A guide to the project and to the field

Solar System Simulator

The complete guide: physics, numerical methods, NASA data and the code that ties them together

This document explains everything in this project: what each file does, the physics behind every line, and why it's built the way it is. It's also a general introduction to how solar system simulators work. You should be able to read it start to finish and then build one of your own.

Part I

The big picture

1. What a solar system simulator is

An animation moves planets along circles that someone drew. A simulator knows only the laws of physics and a starting moment, and works out everything else. Nobody tells our simulated Earth to go around the Sun. It does so because gravity pulls it and it was already moving sideways at 30 km/s. That difference is the point: a simulator can answer questions nobody drew the answer to, like "where will Jupiter be in 50 years?", "what if the Sun were twice as heavy?" or "would this asteroid survive near Jupiter?".

This project simulates the Sun, the planets, their moons, asteroids and comets. It starts from NASA's real measured positions on a chosen date, moves them forward with Newton's laws, draws the result in 3D, and checks itself against where NASA says things actually were later.

2. The four questions every simulator answers

Every physics simulator, whether planets, pendulums, rockets, galaxies or weather, answers the same four questions. Keep them in separate pieces of code and the whole project stays easy to understand and change.

QuestionIn this projectFiles
1. What exists, and what's its state now?Bodies with mass, position, velocity, loaded from NASAbody.py, data_sources.py, nasa_api.py
2. What rules make things change?Newton's gravity: every body pulls every otherphysics.py
3. How do we move time forward?Velocity Verlet, in small steps dtintegrator.py, simulation.py
4. How do we know it's right?Energy stays constant; matches NASA a year latercheck_accuracy.py

Plus two helpers that aren't physics: drawing (visualize.py, camera.py) and wiring it together (main.py).

3. Quick start

From a terminal in the project folder (Windows PowerShell):

py -3.13 -m venv .venv                 # 1. a private Python just for this project
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1            # 2. switch to it (prompt shows "(.venv)")
pip install -r requirements.txt       # 3. install the packages
python check_accuracy.py              # 4. test the physics against NASA (no window)
python main.py                        # 5. open the 3D view in your browser
python nasa_api.py                    # 6. try the NASA data module on its own
python docs/build_docs.py             # 7. rebuild this guide

What you can change lives in the SETTINGS block at the top of main.py (Appendix B shows its current contents): which planets, which moons, which asteroid searches, the time step and the animation speed.

Part II

The physics

4. Vectors and units

Vectors: arrows with a size and a direction

A position is an arrow from a fixed origin to the object: three numbers r = (x, y, z). A velocity v = (vx, vy, vz) is an arrow saying which way the object moves and how fast. An acceleration a says how the velocity is changing. Bold letters in this guide mean vectors. The length of a vector is written |r| or just r, and it comes from Pythagoras: r = √(x² + y² + z²). In code: np.linalg.norm(r).

Two vector operations appear often:

  • Dot product a·b = axbx + ayby + azbz, which measures "how much do these point the same way". The camera uses it to find where the mouse points (Section 29).
  • Cross product a×b gives a new arrow perpendicular to both (right-hand rule). It's used for angular momentum (Section 8) and the camera's "right" direction.

Units: pick one system and convert at the edges

Inside the simulator everything is SI: metres, seconds, kilograms. Astronomers often use larger units, so we convert only where data enters or leaves:

UnitValueWhere it appears
Astronomical unit (AU)1.495978707 × 1011 m (exact, by definition)NASA's positions; drawing scale
Day86 400 sNASA's velocities (AU/day); animation speed
GMkm3/s2 in NASA tables; m3/s2 in code (× 109)Masses (Section 21)
Why this matters Mixing units is the most common bug in scientific code. A famous real example: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team's software used pound-force seconds and another's expected newton-seconds.

5. Newton's laws of motion

  1. Inertia. Without a force, an object keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed. Planets "want" to fly off in a straight line. Gravity keeps bending their path.
  2. F = m a. A force changes velocity. The same force accelerates a light object more than a heavy one.
  3. Action = reaction. If the Sun pulls Earth, Earth pulls the Sun with an equal and opposite force. The Sun moves much less only because it's 333 000 times heavier.

6. Newton's law of gravitation

Every mass attracts every other mass. The pull points toward the other body, is proportional to both masses, and falls off with the square of the distance: twice as far means a quarter of the pull.

F = G m1 m2 / r²  (toward the other body) G = 6.674 × 10−11 m³ kg−1 s−2  ·  r = distance between the centres

Combine with F = m a. The mass of the body being pulled cancels out, so its acceleration does not depend on its own mass:

ai = G Σj≠i mj (rj − ri) / |rj − ri|³ add up the pull of every other body j on body i
  • Why r³ for an inverse-square law? The top part (rj − ri) is itself one distance long. Dividing by r³ leaves "a direction of length 1" × "1/r²". One formula gives both direction and strength.
  • Superposition: pulls simply add. The pull on Earth = the Sun's pull + the Moon's + Jupiter's + …
  • Own mass cancels: a feather and a planet fall the same way. That's why asteroids can be test particles (Section 9): their motion doesn't depend on their mass.
  • Point masses (shell theorem): Newton proved that a spherical body pulls exactly as if all its mass sat at its centre. So for orbits only the mass and centre matter, and size and spin don't.
In this project physics.accelerations() computes exactly this sum, for every body at once, using NumPy (Section 26). Section 17 explains the cost: every pair of bodies must be considered.

7. The two-body problem and Kepler's laws

With only two bodies (say, Sun and Earth), Newton's equations can be solved exactly with pen and paper. The answer was discovered from observations by Johannes Kepler around 1609–1619, decades before Newton explained why. These are Kepler's three laws.

First law: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus

An ellipse is a stretched circle. Its size is the semimajor axis a (half the longest width) and its stretch is the eccentricity e: 0 = circle, 0.0167 = Earth (almost a circle), 0.97 = Halley's comet. The Sun sits not at the centre but at a focus. The closest point is perihelion, distance a(1 − e), and the farthest is aphelion, a(1 + e). More generally, two-body paths are conic sections: ellipses (bound), parabolas, and hyperbolas (escaping, e.g. interstellar visitor ʻOumuamua).

Second law: equal areas in equal times

The line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fast near the Sun and slow far away. Why: gravity pulls straight toward the Sun, so it can't twist the orbit, and angular momentum L = m r v⊥ stays constant (Section 8). Smaller r forces bigger v. Earth moves 30.3 km/s in January and 29.3 km/s in July.

Third law: T² ∝ a³

T = 2π √( a³ / GM ) T = orbital period · a = semimajor axis · M = mass of the central body (strictly, M + m)

Bigger orbits take longer, and not just because they're longer: the planet also moves slower. Check with Earth: a = 1.496 × 1011 m and GMSun = 1.327 × 1020 m³/s² give T = 3.156 × 107 s = 365.25 days. In "astronomer units" (T in years, a in AU, around the Sun) it becomes simply T² = a³: Jupiter at 5.2 AU takes √(5.2³) ≈ 11.9 years.

Vis-viva: the orbit's size from a single snapshot

Energy conservation gives a relation between speed v at distance r and the orbit size a:

v² = GM ( 2/r − 1/a )   ⇒   a = 1 / ( 2/r − v²/GM )

Two famous special cases: circular speed v = √(GM/r) (for Earth: 29.8 km/s) and escape speed v = √(2GM/r). If 2/r − v²/GM ≤ 0 the body is not bound at all.

How this project uses Kepler's laws
  • physics.orbital_period() takes a moon's position and velocity relative to its planet, gets a from vis-viva, then T from the third law.
  • data_sources.suggest_time_step() uses that period to pick a safe time step: about 1/100 of the fastest orbit (Io: 1.77 days → 25.5 minutes). See Section 16.
  • data_sources.make_moon() uses it again to set each moon's spin, because big moons are tidally locked (Section 11).
  • The simulation doesn't use Kepler's laws to move anything. It uses Newton's law directly, and Kepler's laws come out by themselves. That's a good check: our Earth really does take 365.25 days.

Kepler's laws are exact only for two bodies. With three or more, the bodies tug on each other and the ellipses slowly change (perturbations). That's why we need the N-body approach of Section 9.

8. Conservation laws: the simulator's test suite

In a closed system with only gravity, three totals never change. The simulation does not enforce them. It just follows the forces. So if they drift, the numerical method is making errors. That's how you test a simulator when you don't know the right answer.

QuantityFormulaWhy it's constant
EnergyE = Σ ½ m v² − Σpairs G mi mj / rijNo friction; nothing to lose energy to
MomentumP = Σ m vNewton's 3rd law: internal pulls cancel in pairs
Angular momentumL = Σ m (r × v)Gravity acts along the line between bodies, so no twist

The first term of E is kinetic energy (energy of motion). The second is potential energy, which is negative because the bodies sit in a gravitational "well": you'd have to add energy to separate them to infinity, where potential energy is defined as zero. A planet constantly trades the two: it speeds up as it falls closer, but the sum stays fixed.

In this project physics.py has total_energy, total_momentum and total_angular_momentum. check_accuracy.py reports the relative energy error |E(t) − E₀| / |E₀|. Test particles are excluded from these sums: they get pulled without pulling back, so they're not part of the conserved system.

9. The N-body problem

With three or more bodies there is no general formula. Henri Poincaré showed in the 1890s that the three-body problem is in general chaotic: tiny differences in the start grow until the outcomes are completely different. So we solve it numerically, in small time steps (Part III). That's an N-body simulation, and the method is an N-body integrator.

The barycenter (centre of mass)

The mass-weighted average position R = Σ mr / Σ m. By Newton's laws it moves at constant velocity forever. In the Solar System it's close to the Sun but not at it: Jupiter pulls it to just outside the Sun's surface at times. NASA measures positions from the Solar System Barycenter (SSB).

In this project NASA's coordinates include pulls from bodies we may not simulate (Pluto, thousands of asteroids). Our subset's own centre of mass may then drift slowly across the screen. Simulation.move_to_center_of_mass() subtracts it, so total momentum becomes exactly zero. check_accuracy.py skips this and compares Earth relative to the Sun instead, which doesn't depend on the origin.

Test particles

Objects so light that their pull is negligible. Ceres, the largest asteroid, has about 1/6000 of Earth's mass. We let them feel gravity but skip their pull. In code, their "gravity mass" is set to 0, so no special-case if is needed.

Hierarchical systems

Moons orbit planets that orbit the Sun: an orbit inside an orbit. This matters in two ways: moons force small time steps (Section 16), and a planet's mass must not be counted twice (Section 22).

10. Reference frames and time

  • Ecliptic frame. The x-y plane is the plane of Earth's orbit (the ecliptic). +x points to the March equinox (where the Sun appears on ~20 March). +z is "ecliptic north". Seen from +z, all planets orbit counter-clockwise.
  • Barycentric. The origin is the Solar System Barycenter (Section 9).
  • TDB time. "Barycentric Dynamical Time" is the steady clock used for planetary motion. It differs from everyday UTC by about 69 seconds (leap seconds and relativity).
  • Screen frame. VPython uses y = up on screen. The view draws simulation (x, y, z) at screen (x, z, −y), a pure rotation, so left/right handedness and orbit direction are kept.

11. Spin, axial tilt, seasons and tidal locking

Revolution (going around the Sun) comes from gravity. Rotation (spinning around one's own axis) is a separate motion. Because of the shell theorem (Section 6), spin doesn't change the orbit in this model, so it's simple geometry: angle turned = 360° × elapsed time / rotation period.

  • Sidereal vs solar day. Earth turns once relative to the stars in 23 h 56 m (sidereal). Relative to the Sun it takes 24 h, because Earth moves ~1° along its orbit each day and must turn a bit extra. We use sidereal periods.
  • Axial tilt (obliquity). The angle between the spin axis and the orbit's "north". Earth: 23.44°. Over 90° means the body spins backwards (retrograde): Venus 177.4° (upside down, slowly backwards), Uranus 97.8° (rolling on its side).
  • Seasons. A spinning planet is a gyroscope: its axis points the same way in space all year. In June Earth's north leans toward the Sun (summer), and in December, on the far side of the orbit, it leans away. Seasons are not caused by distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
  • Tidal locking. A planet's gravity stretches a nearby moon slightly. Friction from that stretching slowly brakes the moon's spin until one rotation takes exactly one orbit. That's why we always see the same face of our Moon. Most large moons are locked, so the project sets their spin period equal to their orbital period (Kepler's third law).

12. What this model leaves out

Every model is a simplification. Knowing what's missing tells you how far to trust it.

Missing effectSizeMatters for
General relativity (Einstein's correction to Newton, strongest near the Sun)Mercury's perihelion turns an extra 43″ per century; Earth's position shifts by tens of km per yearThe leftover ~50 km error in our NASA test
Non-spherical shapes (planets bulge at the equator, "J2")Tiny for planets' orbits; large for close moons and satellitesInner moons, spacecraft
Tides (bodies stretching each other)The Moon recedes 3.8 cm/yearMillions of years
Non-gravitational forces (comet outgassing, sunlight pressure, Yarkovsky effect)Significant for comets and small asteroidsComet predictions, asteroid impact risk
CollisionsBodies pass through each other hereClose encounters, planet formation
Part III

Numerical integration: the "N-body integrator"

13. What an integrator is

Physics gives us rates of change, not answers. The position changes at the rate of the velocity, and the velocity changes at the rate of the acceleration:

dr/dt = v      dv/dt = a(r) a pair of differential equations; a comes from gravity (Section 6)

An integrator turns rates into a path. It takes the state (all positions and velocities) at time t and estimates the state at t + dt. Repeat thousands of times and you have the future. The name comes from calculus, where adding up many tiny changes is called integrating.

An N-body integrator is just this machine applied to N gravitating bodies. In the notebook that started this project (N-integral.ipynb) it was a loop with four lines. In this project the same idea is split into "the step method" (integrator.py) and "the forces" (physics.py), so either can be swapped.

Analogy Driving with your eyes closed, opening them for a split second every dt to check which way to steer. The shorter the gaps, the better you follow the road. But a clever steering rule matters even more than the gap length (next two sections).

14. Forward Euler and why orbits spiral

new_pos = pos + vel * dt     # move in a straight line with the OLD velocity
new_vel = vel + acc * dt     # then update the velocity

The simplest method (Leonhard Euler, 1768). Each step moves in a straight line along the current direction. But a straight line that touches a circle always ends up slightly outside it. Every step adds a sliver of energy, and the orbit spirals outward forever. A smaller dt slows the spiral but never stops it.

Measured in this project (Sun + Earth, dt = 1 hour, one year): energy error 1 part in 100, Earth 5 300 000 km away from where NASA says it really was.

15. Velocity Verlet (leapfrog) and symplectic methods

half_vel = vel + 0.5 * dt * acc            # 1. KICK:  half a velocity update (old force)
new_pos  = pos + dt * half_vel             # 2. DRIFT: move with the half-way velocity
new_acc  = accel_func(new_pos)             # 3. compute gravity at the new positions
new_vel  = half_vel + 0.5 * dt * new_acc   # 4. KICK:  other half (new force)

It costs the same as Euler (one gravity calculation per step), but it's time-symmetric: run it backwards and it retraces its path exactly. Methods that preserve the deep geometric structure of Newton's equations (the "phase-space volume") are called symplectic. Their energy error does not build up. It just wobbles slightly and stays bounded for millions of orbits. That's why real planetary codes use this family of methods.

Measured (Sun + Earth, dt = 1 h, 1 year)Energy errorEarth vs NASA
Forward Euler9 × 10−35 300 000 km
Velocity Verlet9 × 10−9 (about 1 million times smaller)1 160 000 km*

* The remaining position error with Verlet is not the integrator's fault. It's missing physics: with only Sun + Earth, nothing pulls Earth the way the Moon, Venus and Jupiter really do. See Part VII.

In this project Both methods live in integrator.py with the same signature step(pos, vel, acc, accel_func, dt) → (new_pos, new_vel, new_acc), so they plug in interchangeably (python check_accuracy.py --integrator euler). Passing acc in and out means gravity is computed only once per step: step 3's result is exactly what the next step's step 1 needs.

16. Errors and choosing the time step

  • Truncation error: the error from replacing a smooth curve with straight pieces. Euler is a first-order method (halving dt roughly halves its error). Verlet is second-order (halving dt roughly quarters it).
  • Round-off error: computers store about 16 significant digits. Billions of tiny steps add up their round-off, so infinitely small dt isn't the answer either.
  • Rule of thumb: at least ~100 steps per orbit of the fastest body. Then halve dt and check the answer barely changes. If it changes a lot, dt was too big.
Fastest bodyIts orbitSafe dt (÷ 100)
Earth around the Sun365.25 days~3.7 days (we use 1 hour anyway)
Moon around Earth27.3 days~6.5 hours
Io around Jupiter1.77 days~25 minutes
Phobos around Mars7.65 hours~4.6 minutes (slow to run!)
In this project main.py calls suggest_time_step() and automatically shrinks DT_HOURS if a fast moon needs it, printing which moon forced the change. The fastest body sets the pace for everyone: that's why the book's later chapters introduce adaptive and per-body time steps.

17. Speed: the N² problem

Each body feels every other body, so N bodies have about N² pairs. 30 bodies = 900 pairs per step, which is trivial. 100 000 stars = 10 billion pairs per step, which is not. Three tools keep it manageable:

  • Vectorization (used here): NumPy computes all pairs in one operation in compiled C, about 50–100× faster than Python loops.
  • Test particles (used here): massless bodies cost (planets × all) instead of (all × all), so thousands of asteroids are cheap.
  • Approximation (not used here): the Barnes–Hut tree method treats a distant cluster as one mass (N log N); galaxy simulations use this, often on GPUs.

18. Beyond this project: better integrators

MethodIdeaWhen to use
Runge–Kutta 4 (RK4)Samples the slope 4 times per step and averagesVery accurate short runs; energy drifts slowly over long ones
Adaptive step (RKF45, Dormand–Prince)Estimates its own error and grows/shrinks dtComets and close encounters, where speed changes a lot
IAS15 (Gauss–Radau, 15th order)Very high-order with automatic steps; errors at round-off levelResearch-grade accuracy (used in REBOUND)
Wisdom–HolmanSolves each planet's Kepler ellipse exactly and adds planet–planet tugs as kicksMillions of years of Solar System evolution

The book Moving Planets Around (in this folder) builds these step by step: Euler (Ch. 3), conservation checks (Ch. 4), RK4/leapfrog/symplectic (Ch. 5), adaptive steps (Ch. 6), N bodies (Ch. 7), IAS15 (Ch. 8), Wisdom–Holman (Ch. 9).

Part IV

Real data from NASA/JPL

19. Where the numbers come from

Gravity tells you how things move. The initial conditions (positions and velocities at a starting moment) tell you what the orbits are. Two identical Earths with different starting speeds trace completely different paths. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) tracks the Solar System with radar, spacecraft and telescopes, and publishes it for free, with no API key. NASA has no single "everything" API, so this project combines several official sources:

WhatJPL sourceUsed by
Positions and velocities on any dateHorizons API (via the astroquery package)data_sources.fetch_state_vector
Every moon of every planetHorizons "major body" (MB) indexnasa_api.list_moons
Moon masses (GM), radii, densitiesPlanetary Satellite Physical Parameters pagenasa_api.moon_physical_data
Planet mass without its moonsSame page, second tablenasa_api.planet_gm_without_moons
Asteroid and comet search (1.5 million+)Small-Body Database (SBDB) Query APInasa_api.query_small_bodies
Find any object by nameHorizons Lookup APInasa_api.lookup
Planet sizes, spin periods, tiltsNASA Planetary Fact Sheet (typed into a table)data_sources.PHYSICAL_DATA
Caching Every download is saved: positions in data/horizons_cache.json, everything else in data/nasa_cache/. The second run is instant, works offline, and doesn't burden NASA's servers. Delete the files (or pass refresh=True) to fetch fresh data. Always cache slow or remote data in scientific code.

20. JPL Horizons: positions and velocities

We ask Horizons for state vectors with three settings: location="500@0" (measure from the Solar System Barycenter), refplane="ecliptic" (the ecliptic frame), and the date in the TDB time scale (Section 10). Horizons answers in AU and AU/day, and we convert to metres and m/s.

Horizons ID numbers

IDMeaningExample
0Solar System Barycenter
1–9Planet system barycenter (planet + its moons as one point)5 = Jupiter system
10The Sun
X99Planet X's own body399 Earth, 599 Jupiter
X01–X98, X5nnnMoons of planet X301 Moon, 501 Io, 55501 (S/2003 J2)
DES=<spkid>;Asteroid by its database ID (a plain number is not accepted; found by testing)DES=20000001; = Ceres
designation + "closest apparition"Comets (each return to the Sun has its own orbit solution)1P = Halley

For Jupiter–Neptune the project normally uses the system barycenter (5–8) with the system GM: if the moons aren't simulated, "planet + moons as one point" is the most accurate stand-in. Section 22 explains what changes when moons are added.

21. Masses: why we store GM

Gravity only ever uses the product G × M. Astronomers measure that product directly from how spacecraft and moons are pulled, to about 11 digits. G by itself is known to only about 5 digits, so "mass in kg" is the less precise number.

A real bug from this project's history The first version stored masses in kg. With all planets included, Earth ended up 88 700 km off after one year. The 0.0045 % error in G × MSun slightly changed every orbit's speed. Switching to JPL's GM values (from the DE440 planetary model) brought it down to 109 km. The code now stores GM and computes mass = GM / G, so G × mass gives NASA's exact GM back. Lesson: store the quantity that is measured most precisely.

22. Moons

nasa_api.list_moons(planet) reads the Horizons major-body index: Earth 1, Mars 2, Jupiter 115, Saturn ~290, Uranus 28, Neptune 16, Pluto 5. JPL has measured masses for about 46 of them. Moons without a mass become test particles.

The double-counting rule Normally Jupiter is simulated as "Jupiter + all its moons" in one point (ID 5, system GM). If you also add Io separately, Io's mass would be counted twice. So when a planet's moons are added, build_system() switches that planet to its own body (ID 599) and its moon-free GM (from planet_gm_without_moons()).

Each moon's spin is set from tidal locking (Section 11). Its orbital period comes from Kepler's laws (Section 7). Io gives 42.5 h = 1.77 days, matching its real orbit.

23. Asteroids and comets

nasa_api.query_small_bodies() searches JPL's Small-Body Database: 1.58 million asteroids and 4 089 comets at the time of writing. You can filter by orbit class, near-Earth only, and sort by size. Fields returned include GM (only for the few with measured masses, like Ceres and Vesta), diameter, spin period, and orbit elements a, e, i.

ClassMeaning
MBAMain belt, between Mars and Jupiter (most asteroids)
APO / ATE / AMO / IEONear-Earth groups: Apollo, Aten, Amor, Atira (by how their orbit relates to Earth's)
TJNJupiter trojans: share Jupiter's orbit, 60° ahead or behind (stable Lagrange points L4/L5)
CEN, TNOCentaurs (between Jupiter and Neptune), trans-Neptunian objects (Kuiper belt)
JFc, HTCJupiter-family comets, Halley-type comets

Measured result: adding the 10 biggest asteroids' gravity changed Earth's one-year position by no measurable amount. Their combined mass is about 1/2000 of Earth's. Name clashes are handled too: asteroid "52 Europa" vs Jupiter's moon Europa keeps its full name.

Part V

The code, file by file

24. Architecture and design principles

  1. Separation of concerns. State, forces, stepping, drawing and data each live in their own file. The integrator never knows it's computing gravity: it just calls "the force function". The same integrator could run a pendulum.
  2. Everything is a Body. The simulator never asks "is this a planet?". Sun, moon, asteroid, comet, or a star you invent are the same type. Adding objects needs no physics changes.
  3. Arrays for speed, objects for clarity. Body objects are easy to read and create. The Simulation copies them into NumPy arrays where the maths happens.
  4. Special cases as data, not ifs. Test particles have gravity-mass 0. A body's distance to itself is set to infinity so 1/∞ = 0. The maths stays fast and simple.
  5. Adapter for messy sources. nasa_api.py hides four different NASA formats behind plain functions. If NASA changes a format, only that file changes.
  6. Physics in true units, drawing in fake ones. Drawing tricks never leak into the maths (Section 28).
  7. Measure, don't eyeball. check_accuracy.py turns "looks right" into numbers.

25. The Python and NumPy toolkit

ConceptWhat it isWhere
Module / importEach .py file is a module; from physics import G borrows a name from another fileeverywhere
Class, object, selfA class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it; self = "this object"Simulation, FlyCamera
@dataclassA class that's mostly a form with named fields and defaultsBody
_nameConvention for "internal, don't call from outside"_pack, _apply
List comprehension[make_body(n, d) for n in names] builds a list in one linemain.py
Functions as valuesPass a function without () so someone else can call it lateraccel_func, INTEGRATORS
if __name__ == "__main__"Run only when the file is executed directly, not when importedscripts
NumPy array, shapeA grid of numbers; positions have shape (N, 3)simulation.py
BroadcastingCombining shapes (1,N,3) and (N,1,3) gives all N×N pairs at oncephysics.accelerations

Broadcasting, slowly

diff = positions[np.newaxis, :, :] - positions[:, np.newaxis, :]   # shape (N, N, 3)
# diff[i, j] = arrow from body i to body j, for ALL pairs, like a multiplication table:
#               rows = "who is pulled", columns = "who pulls"
dist = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=2)      # (N, N) table of distances
np.fill_diagonal(dist, np.inf)           # body-to-itself = infinity, so 1/inf = 0, no self-pull
pull = gravity_masses[None, :, None] * inv_r3[:, :, None] * diff
acc  = G * pull.sum(axis=1)              # add up each row: total pull on each body

26. Every file explained

main.py: the switchboard

Holds the SETTINGS (date, planets, moons, asteroid searches, time step, speed) and wires the pieces together: build_system → suggest_time_step → Simulation → move_to_center_of_mass → SolarSystemView.run(). Short on purpose: it shouldn't contain any physics.

body.py: what one object is

A @dataclass with physics fields (mass, position, velocity, is_test_particle) and drawing-only fields (radius, rotation_period, axial_tilt, color, texture, parent). __post_init__ runs right after creation: it converts vectors to float arrays and rejects bad input early (wrong length, negative mass).

data_sources.py: turning NASA data into Bodies

  • PHYSICAL_DATA: table of Horizons ID, GM, radius, sidereal spin, tilt and colour for the Sun, planets and Moon.
  • fetch_state_vector(): asks Horizons for position and velocity (cached), converts AU → m.
  • make_body(): Sun/planet/Moon Body; with without_moons_gm switches to the planet's own body (Section 22).
  • make_moon(), make_small_body_from_record(), make_small_body(): moons, asteroids, comets.
  • build_system(): assembles everything from the settings and applies the double-counting rule.
  • suggest_time_step(): Kepler-based safe dt (Section 16).

nasa_api.py: the adapter to NASA

list_moons, moon_physical_data, planet_gm_without_moons, query_small_bodies, count_small_bodies, lookup. Uses only Python's standard library: urllib to download, json, and a small HTMLParser subclass to read JPL's tables. Run python nasa_api.py for a demo.

simulation.py: the manager

  • _pack(): copies Bodies into arrays: positions (N,3), velocities (N,3), masses, and gravity_masses (0 for test particles). Also computes the first accelerations.
  • add_body(): the door for new objects, even mid-run.
  • move_to_center_of_mass(): removes centre-of-mass position and velocity (Section 9).
  • step(n): the heartbeat: calls the integrator n times, adds dt to the clock.
  • sync_bodies(), energy(), momentum(), angular_momentum().

physics.py: the rules

accelerations() (Newton's gravity for all pairs), the conservation-law totals, and orbital_period() (vis-viva + Kepler's third law). The only file that knows what gravity is.

integrator.py: moving time forward

forward_euler_step and velocity_verlet_step with identical signatures, plus the INTEGRATORS dictionary so they can be chosen by name.

visualize.py: the 3D view

SolarSystemView creates one VPython sphere per body (with tilt, texture and label), the HUD, the sidebar controls (pause, time speed, follow menu, overview, flight speed, camera glide, trail and display switches) and the animation loop run(). It hands the specialised jobs to the four files below. Details in Section 28.

camera.py: the free-flying camera

FlyCamera stores its own position, yaw, pitch, velocity and turn rates, turns key presses into smoothed thrust (inertia), runs smooth Follow/Overview flights, and positions VPython's camera. Details in Section 29.

trails.py: orbit trails

OrbitTrails records each body's drawn position about 180 times per orbit and removes points older than 2 orbital periods (periods from Kepler's third law), or keeps the full history when switched on. It also keeps every trail about 1.5 pixels wide (Section 28).

starfield.py: background stars

StarField builds 1,500 tiny glowing boxes, 40% of them in a Milky-Way band, as one compound object that travels with the camera (a "skybox", Section 28).

ui_theme.py: the page layout

One block of CSS and JavaScript sent through VPython's caption. It makes the 3D view fill the window, turns the caption into the slide-out sidebar and the title into the HUD, and turns the mouse wheel into thrust (Sections 28–29).

check_accuracy.py: proving it's right

Runs a simulation with no graphics, tracks energy, then compares Earth's position (relative to the Sun) with NASA's after the run. Options: --bodies, --start, --days, --dt-hours, --integrator, --asteroids.

docs/build_docs.py: this guide

Builds this PDF from docs/source/guide.html and fills in the generated appendices. --check lists code that changed since the guide was last built.

27. One frame, traced end to end

view.run()  ── a new frame begins (at 10 days/s and 60 frames/s it owes 4 hours)
   ├─► sim.step(n) ───────────── repeated n times (n = owed time / dt):
   │      └─► velocity_verlet_step
   │             1. kick  (half velocity change)
   │             2. drift (move)
   │             3. accelerations()  ◄── gravity: who pulls whom, how hard
   │             4. kick  (other half)
   │           clock += dt
   ├─► _redraw()               move spheres, spin them, move labels
   ├─► trails.update()         add a trail point if due; drop points older than 2 orbits
   ├─► camera.update()         read keys/mouse, smooth thrust and turning, place VPython's camera
   ├─► stars.follow()          re-centre the star sphere on the camera
   ├─► trails.update_widths()  keep each trail ~1.5 px wide (every 6th frame)
   ├─► _update_hud()           date, speed, what you're following
   └─► rate(60)                wait so we draw at most 60 frames per second

Time debt: each frame adds days_per_second × 1 day / 60 to a "debt" and pays it off in whole steps of dt. The remainder carries over, so even very slow speeds (less than one step per frame) run at the correct average rate. Simulation time and screen time are separate clocks, and this is the link between them.

Part VI

Drawing it: visualization and camera

28. The 3D view

The scale problem

Space is almost empty. If Earth's orbit were a 10 m wide circle, Earth would be a 0.4 mm speck and the Sun a 9 cm ball. Every planetarium cheats, and so do we, only when drawing:

  • Distances: 1 AU = 10 screen units (shrunk evenly).
  • Sizes: enlarged and compressed with a square root. Jupiter (11× Earth's width) is drawn only √11 ≈ 3.3× wider. The Sun is capped so it doesn't swallow Mercury. There's a minimum size so 20 km moons stay visible.
  • Moons: drawn 30× farther from their planet than reality, or they'd hide inside the enlarged planet.

Light, spin, tilt

  • The default lights are removed and a single light is placed at the Sun, so every body has a real day and night side.
  • Each sphere is tilted once by its axial tilt, then each frame turned by 2π × elapsed / rotation period about that axis. VPython's rotate() uses the right-hand rule, so positive angles are counter-clockwise seen from the north, which is how Earth spins.

The page: full window, HUD and sidebar

VPython draws everything in a browser tab with three parts: a title above the 3D view, the view, and a caption below it. ui_theme.py sends one block of CSS and JavaScript through the caption (VPython inserts caption text with jQuery's .append(), which also runs scripts). The script stretches the 3D canvas and its transparent label overlay to the window, turns the caption into a sidebar that slides in from the right (☰ button or H; Esc closes it), and turns the title into a HUD in the top-left corner (date, speed, followed body). Two discoveries from testing the live page: VPython copies the title and caption into new <div>s (so those are what get styled), and it also creates a hidden default canvas (so the script picks the canvas that's actually on the page). After you click a slider, the script hands the keyboard back to the page, or the arrow keys would move the slider instead of the camera.

The starfield: a skybox

Real stars are so far away that crossing the whole Solar System doesn't shift them (no parallax: the nearest star is ~270,000 AU away). starfield.py fakes this with a skybox: a sphere of 1,500 tiny glowing dots that is always centred on the camera, so it travels with you and the stars never get closer, but turning shows different stars. About 40% of the dots are pulled toward a plane tilted 60° to the ecliptic, roughly the real angle of the Milky Way band (our galaxy is a flat disc and we're inside it). Because of the clipping trap (Section 29) the sphere's radius is kept at 4× the camera's look distance and rescaled when that changes. All dots are one compound object, so moving them costs one update per frame.

Trails: two orbits, or the full history

Each body leaves a trail. By default it shows only the last two orbits, so the view never turns into a scribble. Tick Full trail history in the sidebar to keep everything (up to 20,000 points per body). Show trails and Clear trails are there too.

  • Two orbits, not N points. A fixed number of points covers very different amounts of time at different speeds. At 10 days/s Io circles Jupiter in about 10 frames, so 360 points would be ~36 orbits. So every point stores the simulated time it was recorded, and points older than 2 × the body's orbital period are removed.
  • Periods from Kepler's third law. orbital_period() (Section 7) gives each period from the body's position and velocity relative to what it orbits: the parent planet for moons, the Sun for everything else. Measured: Earth 364.8 days, Moon 27.29, Io 1.77. A test at 0.5, 10 and 100 days/s kept 1.9–2.0 orbits every time.
  • Thin at any distance. A VPython curve is a 3D tube, so perspective makes a fixed thickness look fat up close and invisible far away. (Two dead ends found in testing: radius=0 picks a thickness from the view size, and points measure "pixels" at the look point's distance, not at each dot.) The fix is perspective in reverse: something at distance d looks size / d big, so each trail's radius is set to 0.0018 × its body's distance from the camera, giving about 1.5 pixels around the body. Trails glow (emissive), so the Sun's lighting doesn't darken them.

29. The free-flying camera

VPython's built-in camera always orbits a fixed point. camera.py replaces it with a spaceship-style camera.

ControlAction
W / S, A / D, E (or Space) / QThrust forward/back, left/right, up/down
Arrow keysTurn left/right, look up/down
Hold left mouseSteer toward the pointer (further from centre = faster turn)
Mouse wheel (or PageUp/PageDown), ShiftA short glide forward/back (~1.55× closer/farther per click); 5× faster
Follow menu, Overview buttonSmooth flight to any body and ride along with it; smooth flight back to the full view
Flight speed, Camera glide sliders0.1–10× top speed; how long the camera takes to speed up and coast to a stop

Inertia: why it feels like space

A spacecraft doesn't start or stop instantly. The keys don't move the camera directly. They set a target velocity, and the actual velocity closes part of the gap every frame:

v ← v + (vtarget − v) × (1 − e−dt / τ) τ = "Camera glide" (default 0.45 s) · after τ the gap has closed 63%, after 3τ 95%

This is exponential smoothing, a damped motion. You accelerate gently, and when you let go you coast to a stop instead of halting dead. Using e−dt/τ instead of a fixed fraction per frame keeps the feel the same even if the frame rate changes. Turning works the same way with a smoothed turn rate (τ = 0.2 s), and Follow/Overview flights cover a fraction of the remaining distance each frame (τ = 0.55 s), so they speed away and then ease gently into place. A truly frictionless craft would coast forever, which is very hard to steer, so the gentle damping is a deliberate compromise most space games make.

A lesson in exponential growth (found in testing) Top speed is proportional to the distance to the nearest object. So flying away raises your speed, which carries you farther, which raises it again: the distance grows exponentially, like compound interest. With a strong wheel boost, one second of scrolling back flew the camera thousands of times farther out. The fix was a gentler wheel (boost 1.5). Each click then multiplies the distance by a roughly fixed ratio (measured: ~1.55×), which is exactly how a zoom should feel. Flying toward a planet is the mirror image: the distance shrinks exponentially, so you slow down as you arrive and never overshoot. A per-frame limit (at most half the gap to the nearest object) guarantees you can't pass through a planet in one frame.

How the camera works

  • Yaw and pitch: the direction is stored as two angles (turning the body, tilting the head). Each frame they become three arrows, forward, right (forward × up) and up, and the keys move along them. Pitch stops at 89° because straight up makes "right" undefined.
  • Adaptive speed: flying speed is proportional to the distance to the nearest object, so you creep near planets and race through empty space (the trick Celestia and SpaceEngine use).
  • The clipping trap: VPython only draws objects between d/100 and 10d from the camera, where d is the distance to its look-at point (found in VPython's own source code). So the look-at point is kept at 10× the nearest object's distance.
  • Why steering, not dragging: VPython reports the mouse a frame or two late. "Turn by how far the mouse moved" would then feed back on itself and jitter. "Turn rate proportional to the pointer offset" is immune to the delay.
  • Following: each frame the camera moves by however much the target moved, so you can still fly around it while riding along.
Part VII

Is it right? Validation

30. Testing against reality

check_accuracy.py runs two tests without graphics:

  1. Conservation test: does total energy stay constant? This tests the integrator.
  2. Reality test: start from NASA's real state on a date, simulate one year, and compare Earth's position relative to the Sun with NASA's real one a year later. This tests physics and data together.
Setup (start 2026-01-01, 1 year)Energy errorEarth vs NASA
Sun + Earth, Euler, dt = 1 h~1 × 10−2~5 300 000 km
Sun + Earth, Verlet, dt = 1 h~1 × 10−8~1 160 000 km
All planets + Moon, masses in kg (old bug)~5 × 10−9~88 700 km
All planets + Moon, NASA GM, dt = 1 h~5 × 10−9~109 km
Same, dt = 15 min~3 × 10−10~50 km
Same + 10 biggest asteroids~3 × 10−10~50 km (no change)

Reading the table: 50 km after a journey of about 940 million km is an error of 0.000005 %. The remaining gap is mostly general relativity (Section 12), which a Newtonian code cannot capture. The table also shows why each design decision exists: Verlet over Euler, all planets, GM over kg.

Experiments to try (predict first, then run) python check_accuracy.py --dt-hours 0.5  ·  --integrator euler  ·  --days 3650  ·  --bodies Sun Earth Moon  ·  --bodies Sun Earth Jupiter. Which single planet matters most for Earth? When your prediction is wrong, find out why. That's how intuition is built.
Part VIII

Going further

31. Extending the project

You want to…Change
Add planets, moons, asteroid searchesOnly the SETTINGS in main.py
Add PlutoOne row in PHYSICAL_DATA (ID 9, GM ≈ 975.5, radius 1188.3 km, spin 153.29 h, tilt 122.53°)
Invent a body (a rogue star)Create a Body(...) and call sim.add_body()
Add a force (relativity, thrust)Add a term in physics.accelerations; the integrator is untouched
Add an integrator (RK4)A new function with the standard signature in integrator.py + an INTEGRATORS entry
Add a data sourceA function in nasa_api.py that returns plain dicts

A ladder of practice simulators (same structure, different rules)

  1. Pendulum: force = −(g/L) sin θ. The same Verlet step works on any force.
  2. Masses on springs: Hooke's law; watch energy swap between motion and stretch.
  3. Binary star with a planet: two Sun-mass bodies. Can the planet survive? (The book's research project, Ch. 11–13.)
  4. Galaxy collision: thousands of bodies plus softening (add a small ε² to r²) so close passes don't explode.
  5. Rocket to Mars: a spacecraft test particle with thrust; find a launch window.
  6. Charged particles: Coulomb's law has the same 1/r² shape, but like charges repel.

33. Glossary

AUAstronomical unit, 149.6 million km, the average Earth–Sun distance
BarycenterCentre of mass, the balance point of a group of bodies
EclipticThe plane of Earth's orbit; our x-y plane
Eccentricity (e)How stretched an orbit is: 0 circle, <1 ellipse, ≥1 escape
GMGravitational constant × mass; the precisely measured "pulling strength"
Initial conditionsAll positions and velocities at the starting moment
IntegratorAlgorithm that advances the state by one time step
N-body problemPredicting the motion of N mutually gravitating bodies; no general formula for N ≥ 3
ObliquityAxial tilt relative to the orbit
Perihelion / aphelionClosest / farthest point of an orbit around the Sun
Semimajor axis (a)Half the longest width of an orbit, its "size"
SiderealMeasured relative to the distant stars
State vectorPosition + velocity (6 numbers per body)
SymplecticIntegrator type whose energy error stays bounded instead of drifting
TDBBarycentric Dynamical Time, the time scale of planetary ephemerides
Test particleBody that feels gravity but is too light to pull on others
Tidal lockingSpin slowed until one rotation = one orbit
Vis-vivav² = GM(2/r − 1/a), linking speed, distance and orbit size

34. Further reading

  • Moving Planets Around: An Introduction to N-Body Simulations Applied to Exoplanetary Systems (Javier Roa, Adrian S. Hamers, Maxwell X. Cai and Nathan W. C. Leigh; MIT Press 2020, open access under CC BY-NC 4.0; the PDF is in this folder). The textbook this project follows: physics background (Ch. 2), first code (Ch. 3), accuracy (Ch. 4), integrators (Ch. 5–9), production code (Ch. 10), a research project (Ch. 11–14).
  • REBOUND: research-grade open-source N-body code (Python and C) with IAS15 and Wisdom–Holman.
  • Astropy: units, times and coordinate frames done properly. Skyfield: precise "where is it in my sky" positions.
  • JPL Solar System Dynamics (ssd.jpl.nasa.gov): Horizons, the Small-Body Database and the API documentation.
  • Maths worth learning next: vectors and the cross product, ordinary differential equations, basic numerical analysis.

physics.py

physics.py - Newtonian gravity for any number of bodies.

accelerations(positions, gravity_masses)
Gravitational acceleration of every body due to every other body.
kinetic_energy(velocities, gravity_masses)
Energy of motion: sum of 1/2 m v^2 (joules).
potential_energy(positions, gravity_masses)
Gravitational binding energy: sum over each PAIR of -G m_i m_j / r_ij.
total_energy(positions, velocities, gravity_masses)
Kinetic + potential. For a bound orbit this total is negative. A planet trades between the two: it speeds up (more kinetic) as it falls closer (more negative potential), but the SUM stays fixed.
total_momentum(velocities, gravity_masses)
sum of m * v (kg m/s). Newton's 3rd law: every pull has an equal and opposite pull back, so the total never changes.
orbital_period(rel_position, rel_velocity, mu)
How long one orbit takes (seconds), for a body moving around a central body. Uses the position and velocity RELATIVE to that central body. mu = G * (M_central + m_orbiting), m^3/s^2.
total_angular_momentum(positions, velocities, gravity_masses)
sum of m * (r x v). Roughly "how much the system is spinning". Conserving it is why planets move faster when close to the Sun (Kepler's 2nd law: equal areas in equal times).

Simulation.__init__(self, bodies, dt, integrator=velocity_verlet_step)
bodies : list of Body dt : time step in seconds. It must be MUCH smaller than the fastest orbit in the system (rule of thumb: about 1/100 of it or less). Earth's year = 3.2e7 s, the Moon's month = 2.4e6 s, so 1 hour (3600 s) is safe for both. integrator : any function from integrator.py
Simulation.add_body(self, body: Body)
The way to bring new objects in: asteroids, comets, a rogue star... Can be called before running or in the middle of a run.
Simulation.index(self, name)
Simulation.move_to_center_of_mass(self)
Shift positions and velocities so the balance point of OUR bodies sits still at the origin.
Simulation.step(self, n_steps=1)
Advance the simulation by n_steps * dt seconds.
Simulation.sync_bodies(self)
Copy the live arrays back into the Body objects.
Simulation.energy(self)
Simulation.momentum(self)
Simulation.angular_momentum(self)

Copied from the SETTINGS block of main.py when this guide was built.

# ============================== SETTINGS ===================================
START_DATE = "2026-01-01"   # real NASA positions on this date

# BODY_NAMES = ["Sun", "Earth"]

BODY_NAMES = ["Sun", "Mercury", "Venus", "Earth", "Moon", "Mars",
              "Jupiter", "Saturn", "Uranus", "Neptune"]

# Moons of other planets, fetched from NASA. For each planet, give:
#   a list of names  -> just those moons
#   "measured"       -> every moon whose mass JPL has measured (the big ones)
#   "all"            -> every moon NASA tracks (Saturn alone has ~290!)
# Try:  python -c "import nasa_api; print(nasa_api.list_moons('Saturn'))"
MOONS = {
    "Jupiter": ["Io", "Europa", "Ganymede", "Callisto"],   # the 4 Galilean moons
    "Saturn": ["Titan", "Rhea", "Iapetus"],
    # "Mars": ["Phobos", "Deimos"],  # WARNING: Phobos orbits in 7.7 h -> tiny dt -> slow
    # "Uranus": "measured",
    # "Neptune": ["Triton"],
}

# Asteroid/comet searches in JPL's Small-Body Database (see nasa_api.py).
SMALL_BODY_QUERIES = [
    {"kind": "asteroid", "limit": 10},                        # the 10 biggest asteroids
    # {"kind": "asteroid", "sb_class": "TJN", "limit": 20},    # Jupiter trojans
    # {"kind": "asteroid", "near_earth": True, "limit": 20},   # biggest near-Earth asteroids
    # {"kind": "comet", "limit": 5},                           # 5 biggest comets
]

# Hand-picked extras as (Horizons designation, display name).
